entries.clue: Chatter about latest in sportswear with purchaser, chirpy type (11)

indicatorNotes.about: A piece put about another is wrapped round it, so the letters in hand open up to take what is named next.
indicatorNotes.latest in: The latest letter in a word is the one furthest along it, so only the closing letter of sportswear is wanted.

blocks.note: gas is idle talk, the chatter of someone who will not stop
the final letter of sportswear
a purchaser in a shop is a shopper

annotation.surface: Gossip about the newest thing in sports kit, exchanged with a customer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chatter' is the noun gas, idle talk, rather than a person who chatters. 'Chirpy type' wants to be a cheerful sort and is an insect that sings by rubbing its legs.
annotation.definitionFit: A grasshopper chirps all summer by scraping its hind legs against its wings, so the definition names it by its noise.

entries.clue: Her garden she maps out with small area set aside for dogs (6,9)

indicatorNotes.out: To set something out is to lay its parts down in a fresh arrangement, and these letters are laid down in a new one.
indicatorNotes.set aside: What is set aside is put out of the way, so the letter named beside it takes no part in what is built.

blocks.note: sixteen letters to work from, one more than the grid has room for
a is the symbol for the are, the small metric land measure of a hundred square metres, and that letter is the one that goes

annotation.surface: A woman sketching a plan of her garden and leaving a corner of it for the dogs.
annotation.walkthrough: Fifteen-letter fodder spread across four ordinary words is the hardest kind to spot, and every word before 'out' is raw material. The breed is named for the German sheep-herding dogs the type was standardised from in the 1890s.
annotation.definitionFit: German shepherds are a dog breed, so the bare plural 'dogs' covers them as one kind among many.

entries.clue: Fuss about worship (5)

blocks.note: ado is fuss, as in much ado about nothing
re is the about of a memo heading or a subject line

annotation.surface: A great deal of fuss is being made over an act of worship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as the preposition holding the clue together and is two letters to be written down. The definition is the verb: to adore is to worship, whether a god or a person.
annotation.definitionFit: To adore is to worship — the verb used of gods in church and of people loved past all reason.

entries.clue: Nurse running around in the morning to get personal label (7)

indicatorNotes.running: A nurse running is not standing still, and the letters beside the word will not stand in the order they were given either.
indicatorNotes.around: To go around a thing is to close over it, so the loose letters end up on both sides of the piece named next.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
am is the clock's mark for the morning hours

annotation.surface: A nurse dashing about the ward first thing in the morning.
annotation.walkthrough: The same word opens 9 across, where it is a definition rather than fodder — worth noticing how differently a setter can use one word in a single puzzle. 'Personal label' is a mild way of saying the name you inherit rather than choose.
annotation.definitionFit: A surname is the family name a person is filed under on every form and register, the label attached to them for life.

entries.clue: Old French friend about to arrange creative work (7)

indicatorNotes.about: To be about a thing is to be round it, so the two pieces already in hand close over what is clued next.

blocks.note: o is the standard short form of old
ami is French for friend
to rig something is to arrange it, with a hint of fixing the outcome

annotation.surface: An old friend from France is about to organise something artistic.
annotation.walkthrough: The friend does not sit beside the single letter but is separated from it: the two of them wrap round the arranging word, one letter in front and three behind. Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes.
annotation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into birds and boxes, creative work in the plainest sense of both words.

entries.clue: Characters associated with a local area (8)

annotation.definition: Characters associated with a local area

blocks.note: on the surface the colourful people a neighbourhood is known for; in the answer, letters and figures on a page
a British one names the town in its first letters and then narrows to a street or part of one

annotation.surface: The colourful locals who give a neighbourhood its reputation.
annotation.walkthrough: No letters change hands anywhere. 'Characters' is the whole trick, the typographic sense doing duty for the human one, and the rest of the clue is a plain description of what the Post Office hands out.
annotation.definitionFit: A postcode is the short string of letters and figures assigned to one small delivery district, so it is literally characters belonging to a local area.

entries.clue: What to do after a match hastily arranged! (6,2,7)

annotation.definition: What to do after a match hastily arranged!

blocks.note: on the surface a fixture thrown together at short notice; in the proverb, a marriage entered into in haste
the old saying supplies its own second half, which is the answer word for word

annotation.surface: A sporting fixture put together at the last minute, and what follows it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Match' is the marriage sense, the one behind matchmaker, not a game. The proverb runs marry in haste, repent at leisure, and the exclamation mark is the setter pointing at it.
annotation.definitionFit: The proverb 'marry in haste, repent at leisure' ends on the answer, so a marriage rushed into is exactly what leaves you doing it at length.

entries.clue: Commander with weapon wasting little time (6)

indicatorNotes.wasting: What is wasted is thrown away, so the letter named after the word is lost from the one in front of it.

blocks.note: a shotgun is the weapon, seven letters to start from
t is the short form of time, and 'little' marks it as the single letter

annotation.surface: An officer carrying a gun and with no time to spare.
annotation.walkthrough: The shogun was Japan's military ruler for seven centuries, governing while the emperor reigned in name only. The gun survives the clue intact; it is the shot that loses its t.
annotation.definitionFit: The shogun was the supreme military commander of feudal Japan, the man who actually held the army and the country.

entries.clue: Bread Don supplies – just some extra bits (3-3)

indicatorNotes.just some: Just some of the words means a part of them and no more, lifted out in the order it already stands.

blocks.note: six letters running on across two word breaks

annotation.surface: Don is providing the bread, and a few extras alongside it.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on Don makes him a man rather than a don of the common-room kind, which is what keeps the join between the words invisible. The run finishes one letter inside 'supplies'.
annotation.definitionFit: Add-ons are the extra bits bolted on to something already complete — the optional extras on a car or the plug-ins on a program.

entries.clue: Nurse brings support, returning within 60 minutes (7)

indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning comes back along the way it went, so those letters are read in the opposite direction.
indicatorNotes.within: To be within a thing is to sit inside it, so that piece is buried in the middle of the other rather than beside it.

blocks.note: sixty minutes make an hour
the support is a bra, turned back to front

annotation.surface: A nurse fetches some support and is back on the ward inside the hour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' looks like the person at the bedside and is the verb: you nurse a grudge, you harbour one, and either way you keep it going. The support is underwear.
annotation.definitionFit: To harbour a feeling is to nurse it, sheltering it and keeping it alive, just as a harbour shelters ships.

entries.clue: Greek character beset by awful din is dull (7)

indicatorNotes.beset by: To be beset by something is to be hemmed in on every side by it, so this piece finishes up enclosed.
indicatorNotes.awful: An awful din is a disordered one, and the letters it is spelt with come out in disorder too.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, the small word pulled in with the noun
pi is the sixteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

annotation.surface: A Greek is hemmed in by a dreadful racket.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter of the alphabet and 'Greek' says which alphabet to look in. The little word 'is' is quietly part of the fodder, which is what makes the letter count work.
annotation.definitionFit: Insipid means flat and without flavour, and by extension dull — of food, of writing or of company.

entries.clue: A gut upset by a meal cooked in the country (9)

indicatorNotes.upset: A gut that is upset has been churned about, and so have the letters of the word.
indicatorNotes.cooked: A meal cooked has had its ingredients worked into something that looks nothing like them, letters included.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder
five more, making nine in all

annotation.surface: Indigestion brought on by something eaten out in the countryside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the country' reads as where the meal was eaten and is the definition. Each half of the fodder is given its own stirring word, and the two halves simply run together.
annotation.definitionFit: Guatemala is a republic in Central America, one country among many, which is all the bare definition claims.

entries.clue: Piece of poetry penned by American tourist (5)

indicatorNotes.penned by: To be penned by something is to be shut in by it, so these letters are sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: five letters spanning the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: A visitor from the States has written a stretch of verse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penned by' reads as written by and is doing the other sense, the pen that holds animals. A canto is one numbered division of a long poem — Dante's Inferno runs to thirty-four.
annotation.definitionFit: A canto is one of the numbered sections a long poem is built from, so it is literally a piece of poetry.

entries.clue: Home one finally found in North Street (4)

indicatorNotes.finally: What comes finally comes at the very end, so it is the closing letter of the word in front of it.
indicatorNotes.found in: To be found in a place is to be inside it, so that letter goes between the two pieces named next rather than after them.

blocks.note: n is the compass abbreviation for north
the last letter of one
st is how street is written on an address and a signpost

annotation.surface: Somebody is tracked down at last at an address on North Street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home' is the bird's rather than the householder's, which is why a street address is the wrong place to be looking. Two abbreviations stand side by side with a single letter dropped in between.
annotation.definitionFit: A nest is the home a bird builds and comes back to, and the word covers any snug dwelling made by an animal.

entries.clue: Like people serving drinks in prison? (6,4)

blocks.note: bar staff stand on the far side of the counter from everyone they are serving
these bars are the cell's ironwork, and being the wrong side of them is being locked up

annotation.surface: Bar staff pulling pints inside a jail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Serving' works twice over: drinks behind one sort of bar, a sentence behind the other. The question mark is the setter owning up that the barman's version is the looser of the two.
annotation.definitionFit: Bar staff work behind the bar and a prisoner is behind bars, so the same two words cover the pub counter and the cell window.

entries.clue: Once more make caterer agitated before end of dance (8)

indicatorNotes.agitated: A caterer who is agitated has been thoroughly shaken up, and the letters of the word come out in another order.
indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all that is taken from it.
indicatorNotes.before: What comes before a thing is placed in front of it, so the reordered letters lead and the single letter follows.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder
the last letter of dance

annotation.surface: Winding the caterer up just as the dancing comes to a close.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the opening words are free of instructions: 'once more make' is the definition, read as a verb. The dance gives up nothing but its final letter, and that letter goes on the end.
annotation.definitionFit: To recreate something is to make it once more, putting it together again as it was the first time.

entries.clue: Carpe diem spouted by learner concerning early academic course (10)

indicatorNotes.spouted: Words spouted come out in a rush, and these come out in an order other than the one they were written in.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, Horace's tag for seize the day
l is the red plate a British learner driver must display, borrowed by setters for any beginner

annotation.surface: A student quoting Latin about the first stage of a degree.
annotation.walkthrough: Carpe diem is advice on the surface and raw material underneath, the whole tag going into the mix letter for letter. The answer is the adjective, not the course itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Premedical describes the undergraduate study done before medical school proper, so it is the adjective concerning that first course.

entries.clue: Quiet leopard to make swooping attack (6)

blocks.note: p is piano on a score, the composer's mark for playing quietly
the ounce is the snow leopard

annotation.surface: A leopard creeping up in silence before it strikes.
annotation.walkthrough: The ounce is the snow leopard of central Asia, a name now almost confined to crosswords and old natural history, and spelt exactly like the weight. The letter in front comes off a sheet of music.
annotation.definitionFit: To pounce is to drop on prey in one sudden rush from above, which is the swooping attack a cat makes.

entries.clue: One grandma, see, in foolish mode (7)

blocks.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
Nan is what British children call their grandmother
a see is the district a bishop governs, and Ely, the cathedral city in the Cambridgeshire fens, gives its name to one

annotation.surface: Word that one particular grandmother is behaving very foolishly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like the conversational aside its commas make it and is a bishop's territory. English cathedral cities are short and vowel-heavy, so setters reach for them constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: Inanely means in a silly, empty-headed manner, which is what behaving in a foolish mode comes to.

entries.clue: Intransigent pop singer emerging in the eighties (7)

annotation.definition2: pop singer emerging in the eighties

blocks.note: refusing to give an inch, which is the everyday sense of the word

blocks.clueFragment: pop singer emerging in the eighties
blocks.note: a New Romantic stage name of two words, the second an insect, in the charts from 1980

annotation.surface: A stubborn chart act from forty years ago.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is a name rather than a dictionary sense: Adam Ant fronted Adam and the Ants through Stand and Deliver and Prince Charming. Run the two words together and the gap between them disappears.
annotation.definitionFit: Adamant means unyielding, from the old name for the hardest of stones; as two words it is Adam Ant, the British singer who broke through in the early 1980s.

entries.clue: Drink noisily, not quietly, bringing insult (4)

indicatorNotes.not: 'Not' strikes out whatever follows it, so that letter has no place in what is left standing.

blocks.note: to slurp is to drink with a noise
p is piano, the score's mark for quietly, and it is the letter dropped

annotation.surface: Drinking loudly instead of discreetly, and giving offence by it.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves of the wordplay contradict each other on purpose, the noisy drinking supplying the word and the quiet taking a letter out of it. A slur is also the curved line telling a musician to play notes smoothly.
annotation.definitionFit: A slur is a remark that stains someone's name, an insult carrying the weight of slander rather than mere rudeness.

entries.clue: Live wire’s idea’s accommodated (6)

indicatorNotes.accommodated: Something accommodated has been given house room, so these letters are lodged unbroken inside the words in front of the word.

blocks.note: six letters running from the middle of the first word into the second, the apostrophe counting for nothing

annotation.surface: A live wire's suggestion has been taken on board.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Live wire' reads as one phrase for a bundle of energy: in fact the first word is the definition and the second starts the hiding place. The closing 's is standing in for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there, the formal word an official form reaches for when it asks where you are.

entries.clue: The female in old city who will take you to your seat? (5)

annotation.definition: who will take you to your seat?
annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the job by what its holder does instead of offering a noun to swap in; the person it points at is singular, as the answer is.

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a place sits inside it, so the pronoun goes within the letters of the city rather than after them.

blocks.note: Ur was the Sumerian city in what is now southern Iraq, abandoned four thousand years ago
the female pronoun is she

annotation.surface: A woman in an ancient city who shows visitors where to sit.
annotation.walkthrough: Ur is two letters long and genuinely old, which is why setters never let go of it. The question mark covers a definition that describes the job rather than naming it.
annotation.definitionFit: An usher shows an audience to their places in a theatre or cinema, and guests to their pews at a wedding.

entries.clue: Media aces working in educational establishments (9)

indicatorNotes.working: Aces working are being put through their paces rather than left alone, and the letters beside the word are put through a reordering.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Star journalists taking jobs in schools and colleges.
annotation.walkthrough: In England an academy is a state school funded straight from Whitehall rather than through the local council, which is what lets the whole clue read as a plausible news sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Academies are places of learning — in England, state schools run outside local-authority control, and elsewhere colleges of art or music.

entries.clue: Eastern lake is spooky (5)

blocks.note: e is the compass point, east
Erie is one of North America's five Great Lakes

annotation.surface: A lake somewhere out east has an unsettling feel to it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eastern' is doing the compass job rather than saying where the lake is. Erie lies between Ontario and the American Midwest, and its run of vowels makes it a grid-filler's friend.
annotation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange in a way that unnerves you — the spooky feeling of a place that seems to be watching.

entries.clue: My son needs time to make flower arrangement (7)

blocks.note: Cor! and My! are the same British exclamation of surprise
s is the standard abbreviation for son
an age is a long stretch of time

annotation.surface: A parent complains that the boy needs for ever to put the flowers together.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation, the one that pairs with Cor! in British surprise, not the possessive the surface is asking for. A corsage is the small spray pinned to a dress for a wedding or a dance.
annotation.definitionFit: A corsage is a small arrangement of flowers made to be worn, pinned to a dress or tied at the wrist for an occasion.

entries.clue: Silver circle stuck in a difficult place (7)

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum
a round is a circle, the noun for a ring or a circuit

annotation.surface: A silver ring wedged somewhere awkward.
annotation.walkthrough: The chemical symbol is how silver usually reaches a grid, and it comes from argentum rather than from anything in the English word. A ship aground is sitting on the bottom and going nowhere.
annotation.definitionFit: A vessel that runs aground is held fast on the sea bed, and the word carries over to anybody stranded awkwardly.

entries.clue: Two people looking at each other will agree (3,3,2,3)

annotation.definition: Two people looking at each other

blocks.clueFragment: Two people looking at each other
blocks.note: face to face, each eye is level with an eye opposite, which is the phrase read literally
the settled idiom: to be of one mind with somebody about something

annotation.surface: Two people holding each other's gaze.
annotation.walkthrough: The literal half is the joke. Stand face to face and your eyes really are opposite each other, which is all the phrase said before it hardened into an idiom about agreement.
annotation.definitionFit: To see eye to eye with someone is to agree with them, an idiom built on the picture of two people whose eyes meet on the level.
